title: Virtual Memory
tagline: How every program believes it owns the whole machine

sections.content:
Every process on your machine thinks it has exclusive access to a vast, contiguous block of memory starting at address `0x0`. This is **virtual memory** — an illusion maintained by the OS and CPU hardware. In reality, physical RAM is shared among all running processes, and the OS silently maps each process's virtual addresses to physical locations behind the scenes.

Virtual memory solves three critical problems: **isolation** (processes can't read each other's memory), **overcommit** (programs can allocate more memory than physically exists), and **simplicity** (every process gets a clean, uniform address space regardless of hardware layout).

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  VA["Virtual Address\n(process view)"] --> MMU["MMU + Page Table\nLookup"]
  MMU --> TLBhit{"TLB\nHit?"}
  TLBhit -- Yes --> PA["Physical Address\n(RAM frame)"]
  TLBhit -- No --> PT["Walk Page Table\nin RAM"]
  PT --> mapped{"Page\nPresent?"}
  mapped -- Yes --> TLBload["Load TLB entry"]
  TLBload --> PA
  mapped -- No --> PF["Page Fault\n→ OS handler"]
  PF --> disk["Load from Disk\n(swap/file)"]
  disk --> PA
sections.caption: Virtual-to-physical address translation: TLB hit is the fast path; a page fault triggers the OS to load the page from disk.

sections.title: Hotel Room Number Analogy
sections.content:
Imagine every guest at a hotel is given a **room number starting at 1** — each guest believes they have Room 1 through Room N. But the hotel's front desk (the MMU) has a secret ledger mapping each guest's room numbers to actual physical rooms in the building.

Guest A's 'Room 5' might be physical Room 201; Guest B's 'Room 5' is physical Room 547. They never collide. If a guest needs a room that's currently being cleaned (swapped to disk), the front desk pauses them, fetches the room, and then lets them in. The **TLB** is the front desk clerk's mental cache — recently looked-up mappings so they don't consult the full ledger every time.

sections.title: Paging: Breaking Memory Into Fixed-Size Chunks
sections.content:
Virtual memory is managed in fixed-size units called **pages** (typically 4 KB on x86). Physical RAM is divided into equally-sized **frames**. The OS maintains a **page table** per process that maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers. A 64-bit address space has so many possible pages that page tables use multi-level structures (4-level on x86-64) to avoid storing entries for unmapped regions.

The **TLB** (Translation Lookaside Buffer) is a tiny hardware cache inside the CPU that stores the most recently used virtual→physical mappings. A TLB hit resolves an address in 1-2 CPU cycles. A TLB miss triggers a hardware or software page-table walk, costing 10–100+ cycles. A **page fault** occurs when the page isn't in RAM at all — the OS must load it from disk (swap space or a memory-mapped file), which costs millions of cycles.

**Swapping** extends apparent RAM by using disk as overflow. When RAM fills up, the OS evicts the least-recently-used pages to swap space. Excessive swapping (called **thrashing**) causes severe performance degradation as the OS spends more time moving pages than running code.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  PS["Process Stack\n(high addresses)"] --> VAS["Virtual Address Space"]
  PH["Process Heap\n(grows up)"] --> VAS
  PM["Memory-Mapped Files\n/ Shared Libs"] --> VAS
  PC["Code + Data Segment\n(low addresses)"] --> VAS
  VAS --> PT["Page Table"]
  PT --> F1["Frame 0x3A00 (RAM)"]
  PT --> F2["Frame 0x01FF (RAM)"]
  PT --> SW["(swapped to disk)"]
  PT --> F3["Frame 0x7C40 (RAM)"]
sections.caption: A process's virtual address space (stack, heap, code) maps to non-contiguous physical RAM frames via the page table.

sections.explanation: This shows the lazy-allocation nature of virtual memory: `Buffer.allocUnsafe` reserves virtual address space immediately, but physical RAM frames are only mapped when each page is first written (a minor page fault). RSS (Resident Set Size) grows page-by-page as the loop touches memory.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Watch for thrashing:** if `vmstat` or Activity Monitor shows sustained high swap usage and low CPU idle, your system is thrashing. Adding RAM or reducing the working set (data actively accessed) is the fix. No amount of algorithmic optimization helps when the bottleneck is page faults to disk.

items: **Virtual memory** gives each process an isolated, contiguous address space — the OS and MMU silently map virtual addresses to physical RAM frames.
Memory is divided into fixed-size **pages** (usually 4 KB); the OS keeps a **page table** per process mapping virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers.
The **TLB** is a hardware cache for recent page table entries — a hit costs ~1 cycle; a miss costs a full page-table walk; a **page fault** may cost a disk I/O.
**Swapping** lets the OS evict cold pages to disk, enabling programs to use more memory than physical RAM — but excessive swapping causes thrashing.
Physical pages are allocated lazily — virtual address space is reserved on `malloc`, but physical frames are only mapped when a page is first accessed.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of virtual memory?
options: To increase CPU clock speed
To give each process an isolated address space and abstract physical memory layout
To eliminate the need for RAM by using only disk storage
To allow multiple programs to share the same virtual addresses without an OS
quiz.explanation: Virtual memory provides each process with an isolated, uniform address space. The OS maps virtual addresses to physical RAM, hiding hardware layout and preventing processes from accessing each other's memory.

quiz.question: A typical page on an x86 system is how large?
options: 512 bytes
1 KB
4 KB
64 KB
quiz.explanation: The standard page size on x86/x86-64 systems is 4 KB (4096 bytes). Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB) are also supported for workloads with large memory footprints.

quiz.question: What happens during a TLB miss?
options: The process is immediately killed
The CPU performs a page-table walk to find the physical frame, then caches the result in the TLB
The OS swaps the entire process to disk
The virtual address is discarded and the process retries
quiz.explanation: On a TLB miss, the CPU (or OS on a software-managed TLB) walks the page table in RAM to find the mapping. The result is loaded into the TLB so subsequent accesses to the same page are fast.

quiz.question: What is a page fault?
options: A bug in user code that writes to an invalid pointer
When the CPU cannot find a translation in the TLB
When the requested virtual page is not currently mapped to a physical frame in RAM
When two processes try to write the same physical frame simultaneously
quiz.explanation: A page fault occurs when a process accesses a virtual page that isn't currently resident in physical RAM. The OS handler is invoked to load the page — either from swap space or from a file — into a free frame.

quiz.question: What is 'thrashing' in the context of virtual memory?
options: Rapid CPU context switching between many processes
A condition where the OS spends more time swapping pages than executing processes
Memory corruption caused by buffer overflows
Fragmentation of the virtual address space
quiz.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the system's working set (actively used pages) exceeds physical RAM. The OS constantly evicts and reloads pages from disk, spending most of its time on I/O rather than useful computation.

quiz.question: How is a virtual address split into page number and offset?
options: First half = page number, second half = offset, regardless of page size
The top bits identify the page; the bottom log2(PAGE_SIZE) bits are the offset within that page
The OS assigns offsets dynamically at runtime
Page numbers are stored in a separate register from offsets
quiz.explanation: For a 4 KB page, the bottom 12 bits (2^12 = 4096) are the byte offset within the page. The remaining upper bits are the virtual page number looked up in the page table.

quiz.question: Why does a 64-bit page table use multiple levels (e.g., 4-level on x86-64)?
options: To speed up TLB lookups
To avoid allocating a single enormous flat table for a 64-bit address space
Because hardware only supports 32-bit page table entries
To allow different processes to share the same page table
quiz.explanation: A flat single-level page table for a 64-bit address space would require terabytes of memory to store all possible entries. Multi-level tables only allocate intermediate nodes for address ranges that are actually in use.

quiz.question: When a process calls `malloc(1GB)` on a system with only 512 MB of free RAM, what typically happens immediately?
options: The call fails immediately with an out-of-memory error
1 GB of physical RAM is reserved right away
Virtual address space is reserved but physical pages are only allocated as memory is accessed
The OS immediately starts swapping other processes
quiz.explanation: Most OSes use optimistic (lazy) allocation. `malloc` reserves virtual address space immediately but physical frames are only allocated on the first access to each page (demand paging). This is why RSS is often much less than virtual memory size.

quiz.question: What is swap space?
options: A CPU register used to exchange values
A region of disk used to store evicted memory pages when RAM is full
A shared memory region between two processes
Extra VRAM on the GPU
quiz.explanation: Swap space (or a pagefile on Windows) is disk storage the OS uses as an overflow for RAM. When physical memory fills up, the OS writes cold pages to swap so their frames can be reused by other processes.

quiz.question: Which component is responsible for hardware address translation on every memory access?
options: The OS kernel scheduler
The L1 cache
The Memory Management Unit (MMU)
The disk controller
quiz.explanation: The MMU is a hardware unit inside the CPU that automatically translates every virtual memory address to a physical address using the page table and TLB. The OS sets up the page table; the MMU performs the translation transparently on each access.
